svg.aria-label: Diagram: A CloudWatch Logs custom data identifier lets you define your own regular expression in a data protection policy, targeting business-specific PII that managed data identifiers cannot provide, and custom identifiers can be used in conjunction with managed ones. The documented constraint on the pattern is published as a list of permitted characters rather than a named dialect: alphanumerics, the symbols underscore, hash, equals, at, slash, semicolon, comma, hyphen, space, apostrophe and double quote, and the regex reserved characters caret, dollar, question mark, square brackets, braces, pipe, backslash, asterisk, plus and period. The opening and closing parenthesis are not on that list, and parentheses are what grouping, alternation scoped inside a pattern, quantified sequences, capture and non-capturing groups, lookahead and lookbehind are built from, so all of those are unavailable. The pipe is permitted but without parentheses it can only separate whole top-level patterns rather than express a bounded choice. Square brackets give character classes and braces give counted repetition, which covers most fixed-format identifiers, so the practical shape is a flat pattern with a literal anchor, a character class or two, and a count. Excluding parentheses prevents grouped and nested quantified expressions, including some patterns associated with catastrophic backtracking, though AWS documents the supported-character restrictions without stating whether regex performance is the reason for them. The regex has a maximum length of 200 characters, names a maximum of 128 characters restricted to alphanumerics, underscore and hyphen, a custom identifier cannot share a name with a managed data identifier, and a maximum of 10 custom data identifiers are supported for each data protection policy within an overall document limit of 30,720 characters. A custom identifier is a pure pattern with none of the machine learning or keyword proximity inference that managed identifiers use, which means it never misses a detection because a log line lacked a nearby keyword, and equally it cannot distinguish a bare nine-digit employee number from any other nine-digit number, so the context must be written into the pattern as a literal exactly as the AWS example of EmployeeID followed by nine digits does. Custom identifiers may be defined in an account-level policy or in log-group-level policies and the two work in combination, so the effective set for a log group is the union of both.
svg.title: A permitted-character list, and the parenthesis is not on it
svg.text: AWS does not name a regex dialect. It lists the characters you may use.
“RegEx has a maximum length of 200 characters. The following characters are supported …”
Read it for what is absent: there is no ( and no ).
Enough for most fixed-format internal identifiers.
Brackets are a character class, not a group.
Grouped and nested quantified expressions, including some patterns associated with catastrophic
backtracking. AWS documents the character restrictions, not a reason for them.
A custom identifier has no context. You write it in by hand.
Managed identifiers can depend on “keywords in proximity”. A custom one matches exactly what it matches:
it never misses because of phrasing, and it cannot tell your nine-digit ID from any other nine-digit number.
AWS’s own example encodes the fix: EmployeeID-\d{9}. The literal prefix IS the context.
Budget: 10 custom identifiers per policy · names 128 chars, alphanumeric, underscore, hyphen · a name may
not collide with a managed identifier, so the obvious names are already taken · account and log-group sets combine.
A regex is reviewable. When compliance asks what exactly is masked, that is worth more than a category name.
